# Introduction

## Motivation

Raster-to-vector conversion is commonly evaluated according to how accurately a vector
representation reproduces the appearance of the source image. For digital fabrication, however,
visual similarity is not sufficient. A papercraft template contains fabrication information such
as cut boundaries, fold or score lines, individual pieces, physical dimensions, edge labels and
relationships between matching edges.

A vectorization can therefore look almost identical to the source while still being unsuitable
for fabrication: a cut contour is not completely closed, a fold line is classified as a cut line,
two matching edges have different lengths, the physical scale changes, or a label is associated
with the wrong edge.

## Research gap

Existing vectorization research primarily evaluates raster similarity, geometric distance,
contour accuracy and primitive complexity. These measures do not explicitly capture whether the
resulting vector representation is *fabrication-ready*. Papercraft provides a useful experimental
domain because the source documents contain both graphical information and explicit fabrication
semantics.

> There is a lack of benchmark datasets and evaluation methods for assessing raster-to-vector
> conversion when the objective is physical fabrication rather than visual reproduction.

The aim of this study is to develop and evaluate a benchmark framework for fabrication-aware
vectorization using papercraft templates as the application domain. It investigates whether
conventional vectorization metrics adequately represent the properties required for successful
digital fabrication.

## Research questions and hypotheses

- **RQ1 (reconstruction).** How accurately can existing raster-to-vector methods reconstruct the
  geometry of papercraft templates?
- **RQ2 (fabrication semantics).** To what extent do conventional vectorization metrics capture
  fabrication-relevant errors in reconstructed papercraft templates?
- **RQ3 (fabrication-aware evaluation).** Do fabrication-aware metrics provide additional
  information about vectorization quality beyond conventional visual and geometric metrics?

- **H1.** Vectorization methods with similar visual reconstruction accuracy will differ in
  fabrication-relevant correctness; visual fidelity $\neq$ fabrication correctness.
- **H2.** Conventional raster-based similarity metrics will not fully capture topological,
  semantic and dimensional errors relevant to fabrication.
- **H3.** A composite fabrication-aware evaluation will distinguish fabrication-ready
  vectorizations more effectively than visual similarity metrics alone.

## Contributions

- **C1, benchmark.** A curated dataset of papercraft templates with raster inputs and manually
  validated vector ground truth: piece boundaries, cut geometry, fold geometry, physical
  dimensions and edge labels.
- **C2, evaluation framework.** Metrics for properties required for digital fabrication: contour
  closure, topology, dimensional accuracy, cut/fold classification and matching-edge consistency.
- **C3, empirical comparison.** A comparison of existing raster-to-vector approaches on the
  benchmark. The purpose is not a new state-of-the-art vectorizer but to ask how differently
  existing methods behave when evaluated for fabrication rather than visual reproduction.
- **C4, visual versus fabrication quality.** An analysis of whether IoU or Hausdorff distance
  predicts closed contours, matching-edge consistency and dimensional correctness.

# Related work

## Raster-to-vector conversion

Contour extraction [@suzuki1985], line simplification [@douglas1973], curve fitting and
general-purpose tracing [@selinger2003potrace].

## Technical drawing vectorization

@hilaire2006, @noris2013, @bessmeltsev2019 and @egiazarian2020. Papercraft resembles technical
drawings, but differs because graphical elements encode fabrication operations.

## Modern image vectorization

DiffVG [@li2020diffvg], LIVE [@ma2022live] and StarVector [@rodriguez2023starvector] establish
the broader state of image-to-vector research.

Keep this subsection short.

## Vectorization evaluation

Conventional metrics are IoU, Hausdorff distance, raster reconstruction error, primitive count
and path complexity. These metrics primarily measure graphical reconstruction rather than
fabrication validity.

## Digital fabrication requirements

The properties that matter for fabrication are closed geometry, scale, topology, operation
semantics and dimensional consistency, which leads directly into the proposed framework.

# Fabrication-aware vectorization framework

The theoretical proposition is that vector quality has two components,
$Q_{vector} = (Q_{visual}, Q_{fabrication})$, rather than $Q_{vector} = Q_{visual}$
(@fig-framework).

::: {#fig-framework}

```text
Source template
      |
      v
Vectorization
      |
      v
Vector representation
      |
      +---------------+
      v               v
Visual quality    Fabrication quality
 IoU, distance     topology
 pixel error       semantics
 complexity        dimensions
                   validity
```

Visual and fabrication quality are assessed separately on the same vector representation.
:::

# Benchmark and method

## Papercraft dataset

Between 30 and 100 papercraft pages, varying in number of pieces, geometric complexity, fold
density, line styles, labels, page size and raster quality.

::: {.callout-note}
Today there are 21 Bowser pages from one designer, under a personal-use licence and without
ground truth. Synthetic templates (unfolded low-poly meshes rendered with chosen line styles,
then rasterized with controlled degradation) give exact ground truth; real templates serve as the
realism check. The paper must state how the licence allows the real pages to be used.
:::

## Ground-truth annotation

Each template has a manually validated SVG with one group per piece, holding `cut`, `fold` and
`labels` groups, plus JSON metadata for piece dimensions, edge labels and edge matches. The paper
must say how ground truth was made: bootstrapping real pages from the pipeline output biases the
comparison towards baseline D, so every gold page gets an independent full check.

## Vectorization baselines

- **A, simple contour pipeline.** Threshold, contour detection [@suzuki1985], Douglas–Peucker
  [@douglas1973], SVG. A transparent classical baseline.
- **B, general-purpose vectorizer.** Potrace [@selinger2003potrace].
- **C, technical-drawing vectorization.** An existing method with runnable code, for example
  @egiazarian2020; a classical line-extraction method if that is not practical.
- **D, fabrication-aware pipeline.** `lowpoly-pdf-to-svg`, if far enough along. The paper still
  works without D.

Baselines A to C produce untyped paths, so one shared post-classifier labels each path as cut or
fold from the dash pattern of the source under it. It is part of the evaluation protocol, not of
any method, so F3 and F5 are scored the same way for every method.

## Conventional metrics

Raster IoU, $IoU = |R_{GT} \cap R_{pred}| / |R_{GT} \cup R_{pred}|$; Hausdorff distance
$H(A, B)$; mean geometric deviation; number of vector primitives; SVG file size.

## Fabrication-aware metrics {#sec-fab-metrics}

| | Metric | Definition |
|:--|:--|:--|
| F1 | Closed contour validity | $F_{closed} = \text{correctly closed pieces} / \text{total pieces}$ |
| F2 | Dimensional error | $E_{dim} = \lvert L_{pred} - L_{GT} \rvert / L_{GT}$, in % and mm |
| F3 | Cut/fold semantic accuracy | precision, recall, F1 |
| F4 | Topological correctness | missing or extra connections, wrong junctions or holes, disconnected paths |
| F5 | Matching-edge consistency | $E_{match} = \lvert L(e_i) - L(e_j) \rvert$ for edges that should join |
| F6 | Vector complexity | paths, nodes, Bézier control points, SVG size |

: Fabrication-aware metrics. {#tbl-fab-metrics tbl-colwidths="[6,28,66]"}

## Experimental procedure

Each predicted piece is matched to a ground-truth piece by overlap before per-piece metrics are
computed. All metrics are written as one tidy table (`template, page, method, piece, metric,
value`), and the analysis asks whether conventional metrics agree with fabrication-aware ones,
for example $r(IoU, F_{closed})$, $r(IoU, E_{match})$ and $r(Hausdorff, E_{dim})$.

# Results

::: {.callout-note}
Expected pattern, not a claim: two vectorizations with similar visual quality can differ sharply
in fabrication quality. A vectorization with IoU 0.97 and one open contour is unusable for
cutting; one with IoU 0.94, closed contours, correct scale and correct folds is
fabrication-ready. Conventional evaluation prefers the first, fabrication-aware evaluation the
second.
:::

## Failure cases

High IoU but an open contour; low geometric error but a fold classified as a cut; visually
identical but at the wrong physical scale.

# Discussion

## Visual fidelity versus fabrication correctness

Return to the central proposition, visual fidelity $\neq$ fabrication correctness, and explain
which errors conventional metrics miss.

## Implications for vectorization

Evaluation should depend on the intended downstream use. For display,
$Q \approx \text{visual fidelity}$; for fabrication,
$Q = f(\text{geometry}, \text{topology}, \text{semantics}, \text{dimensions})$.

## Implications for digital fabrication

Automatic PDF conversion, Cricut, laser cutting, plotters, CNC workflows and technical drawings.

## Limitations

A relatively small dataset; a papercraft-specific domain; few vectorization baselines; limited
physical fabrication experiments; possible dependence on template conventions; manual
ground-truth annotation.

## Future work

Semantic reconstruction (cut/fold classification, piece detection, OCR); joint reasoning over
geometry, OCR, topology and edge matching; uncertainty-guided human-in-the-loop correction;
learned vectorization; material-aware nesting; larger physical experiments testing whether
fabrication-aware metrics predict assembly success.

# Conclusion

Assuming the results support them: papercraft is a useful benchmark domain for fabrication-aware
vectorization; conventional visual and geometric metrics do not completely characterize
fabrication correctness; and vectorization intended for physical manufacture should explicitly
evaluate geometry, topology, semantics and dimensions.
